extracted.intended_audience: judges, criminalists, forensic physicians, detectives, legal practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for assessing credibility, bias, and reliability of female and child witnesses (and for suspect selection in certain crimes), drawing on medico-legal and psychological observations. Emphasizes practical heuristics—what to ask, how to calibrate testimony, when to suspect particular motives or medical/psychopathological conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid generalizing feminine qualities in examination
rubrics_metrics.description: So long as we stick ... to a concrete instance, and so long as the witness observes no combination of her conduct and opinions with that of the object of her testimony, she will allow herself to be guided partly by the truth, partly by her opinions of the woman in question. But just as soon as we expressly or tacitly suggest common feminine qualities ... she turns about and defends where before she had been attacking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When questioning female witnesses, keep to concrete particulars rather than invoking generalized 'feminine' traits; if the examiner makes the situation 'general' the witness may shift from attacking to defending the accused. Monitor whether your questions have moved the witness into a generalized (and thus biased) frame.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for feminine solidarity/coalition when generalizing
rubrics_metrics.description: But beyond a certain point, women co-operate. This point is easy to find, for it is placed where-ever feminine qualities are to be generalized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that when the topic is framed in terms of shared feminine qualities women may protect one another; use this to explain sudden defensive stances or collective testimony patterns. Seek to determine if testimony reflects personal observation or solidarity-based defense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider women (or effeminate men) first in revenge-motivated crimes
rubrics_metrics.description: When some crime with revenge as motive is before us, and we have no way of getting at the criminal, our first suspicion should be directed toward a woman or an effeminate man.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Feminine hatred is described as more intense and longer-acting than masculine hatred; in crimes where revenge is probable—especially when vengeance far exceeds occasion or occurs after a long delay—prioritize investigating female suspects and weak/effeminate men.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use feminine-character trait clusters to identify perpetrators of cruelty
rubrics_metrics.description: If we succeed, other things being equal, in adducing a number of feminine characteristics with one of which the cruelty of the crime may be connected and explained, we have a clew to the criminal. The instances mentioned,--the motherly care of house and family, frugality, miserliness, hardness to servants, cruelty to aged parents,--seem rare and not altogether rational, yet they occur frequently and give the right clew to the criminal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When cruelty (e.g., cruelty to servants, elderly relatives) appears as motive or explanation, assemble multiple feminine-character indicators (frugality, household devotion, harshness to dependents) as clues rather than relying on a single trait.

rubrics_metrics.name: In poisoning cases prioritize female suspects
rubrics_metrics.description: Every murder, save that by poison, requires courage, the power to do, and physical strength. As woman does not possess these qualities, she spontaneously makes use of poison. Hence, there is nothing extraordinary or significant in this fact ... when there is any doubt as to the murderer in a case of poisoning, it is well to think first of a woman or of a weak, effeminate man.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat poisoning as a mode of murder more likely employed by women (or weak/effeminate men) because it substitutes for physical strength/courage; use this heuristic while still investigating other evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigate suspect's use of popular beliefs and superstitions
rubrics_metrics.description: These circumstances ... require consideration when they count on certain popular views, especially superstitions and certain customs and assumptions. Suppose ... a young wife ... certain proverbs point to the fact that old men who marry young women die soon after marriage ... Therefore a young wife may easily think, 'If I make use of poison nobody will wonder...'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether a suspect might exploit folk-beliefs or superstitions to rationalize or conceal criminal acts; probe the suspect’s knowledge of and reliance on such views as part of motive/capability analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mandate psychiatric/medical examination in child-murder and postpartum cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Such, of course, in particular the former, involve abnormal conditions which are subjects for the physician. ... many a child-murder may possibly be explained by the habit of some animals ... Such cases bind us in every trial for child-murder to have the mental state of the mother thoroughly examined by a psychiatrist, and to interpret everything connected with the matter as psychologist and humanitarian.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require thorough psychiatric/medical evaluation of mothers in filicide cases and consider a broad range of psychopathological and physiological conditions rather than assuming single-category mitigation; do not let statutory leniency preclude careful clinical inquiry into gradations of culpability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not let statutory leniency replace detailed study of child-murder causes
rubrics_metrics.description: Law-makers have without further consideration kept in mind the mental condition of the mother and have made child-murder much less punishable than ordinary murder. It is inferred, therefore, that it is unnecessary to study the conditions which cause it. This is dangerous ... the majority of which we have yet to apprehend and to examine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even where law reduces punishment for filicide due to assumed maternal insanity, judges and experts must still investigate detailed causes and distinctions; avoid blanket assumptions that the case is 'settled' by lesser statutory penalties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess direction and degree of emotional bias in female witnesses
rubrics_metrics.description: We must first of all, when judging her statements, determine the direction in which her emotion impels her ... Nothing will do except a careful study of the specific feminine witness at the time she gives her evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether emotion makes a female witness sympathetic (tending to excuse) or punitive (tending to punish). This requires time: ask comparative questions (including about things you already know) to gauge her 'obliqueness'—but note that these tests show degree, not direction, without careful contextualization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine male and female testimony to approximate an objective average
rubrics_metrics.description: We do best, therefore, when we take the testimony of man and woman together in order to find the right average.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When possible, corroborate female testimony with male testimony; using both can offset opposite biases and give a more reliable composite account. Be careful: differences are not merely quantitative but often qualitative.

rubrics_metrics.name: For uneducated women, judge the form of expression rather than expect mature modes of expression
rubrics_metrics.description: When we inquire into the emotional life of the simple, uneducated women, we find it to be fundamentally the same as that of women of other classes, but different in expression, and it is the expression we have to observe. Its form is often raw, therefore difficult to discover.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjust interpretive approach by social/class background: raw or coarse expression among uneducated women can conceal the same emotional content seen in other classes. Don't mistake coarse expression for different substance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expect women to alter or infer missing elements in secrets/testimony
rubrics_metrics.description: Another consideration of importance is the fact that women who have told secrets have also altered them. This is due to the fact that because they are secrets the whole is not told them and they have had to infer much, or they have not properly understood what was told.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a female witness reports partial information (e.g., a secret), anticipate inferred or altered details; search for illogical elements, identify their logical form, and reconstruct probable original facts. Use detectives’ practice (women often provide leads) but verify inferred parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for feminine intelligence being less logically-constructed
rubrics_metrics.description: It is in matters of intelligence that they fail. ... The feminine intelligence is incapable of logic; she is rather to be persuaded with apparent reasons, with transitory and sparkling matters that have only the semblance of truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that women may be persuaded by apparent, pithy reasons rather than extended logical argument; when assessing consistency and motive, allow for illogical but coherent-seeming justifications that reflect their cognitive style rather than malice or mendacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat children as different in kind, not just degree, from adults
rubrics_metrics.description: The fact is, that because the child is in the process of growth ... it is actually a different kind of being from the adult.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use developmental knowledge when evaluating child witnesses/accused: do not simply scale down adult standards. Specialized studies and approaches (legal medicine, criminal psychology) are required to interpret child testimony properly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discover the child's mental horizon and ideals before relying on testimony
rubrics_metrics.description: If a child is an important witness we can never get the truth from him until we discover what his ideals are. ... the child’s memory constructs new events in terms of his earlier experiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish what the child already knows, their imaginative tendencies and ideals, and how they classify events. Ask grounding questions to map their horizon (city/country exposures, common knowledge) before eliciting decisive testimony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer practical children over clever-unpractical ones as reliable witnesses
rubrics_metrics.description: I should take intelligence only to be of next importance in such cases, and advise giving up separating clever from stupid children in favor of separating practical and unpractical children. ... the least clever practical child is worth more as witness than the most clever unpractical child.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess 'practicality' (ability to observe and reproduce concrete events) as a primary predictor of child witness reliability rather than abstract intelligence scores; prioritize practical children when weighing testimony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious with children’s determinations of time and chronological sequencing
rubrics_metrics.description: Children’s determinations of time are unreliable. Yesterday and to-day are easily confused by small children, and a considerably advanced intelligence is necessary to distinguish between yesterday and a week ago, or even a week and a month.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid relying on precise time references from children without corroboration; individualize questions and contextualize events to the child's temporal framework when establishing chronology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use child testimony for concrete facts but beware of interpretive reconstruction
rubrics_metrics.description: very small children can recall such experiences, though in most cases their recollection is worthless, their circle of ideas being so small that the commonest experiences are excluded from adequate description. But they are worth while considering when a mere fact is in question, or is to be doubted (Were you beaten? Was anybody there? Where did the man stand?).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rely on children for straightforward factual details (presence, simple actions, positions) while treating narrative reconstructions, motives, and complex interpretations with skepticism and requiring corroboration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify interpersonal motives (envy, jealousy, rivalry) as bias sources among female witnesses
rubrics_metrics.description: Envy, dislike, jealousy, and egoism play up vividly, and he is a successful judge who can discover how much of the evidence is born of these motives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate relationships among female witnesses and parties for motives like jealousy or rivalry that could color testimony; employ careful questioning to separate personal motives from objective observation.
